extracted.intended_audience: general readers: aspiring editors, writers, students, and publishing professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive standards for editing across written, visual, audio, and cinematic media, including roles, types of edits, skills required, and technical/pedagogical considerations. Useful for people learning to edit, hiring editors, or understanding editorial workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing is the process of preparing written, visual, audible, or cinematic material with the intention of producing a correct, consistent, accurate and complete final product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modifications can include correcting, condensing, or re-organizing the original material; applies across media and aims at a final product meeting standards of correctness, consistency, accuracy and completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Modifications can include correcting, condensing, or re-organizing the original material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These actions describe concrete interventions an editor may perform; the list signals that edits range from surface corrections to structural reorganizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve authorial intent / know when not to correct
rubrics_metrics.description: An editor must have the knowledge to identify and to correct errors in a piece of work to refine and deliver its message. However, there are times when correcting an error may change the original message of the work. In such cases, editors must also know when to ignore certain errors and to identify the next best possible course of action, which may involve undoing past corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective editing comes from making corrections that still convey the original message; editors should balance correction with respect for the author's intended meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing as collaborative process
rubrics_metrics.description: The editing process often begins with the author's idea for the work itself, continuing as a collaboration between the author and the editor as the work is created.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may work closely with authors through drafts; collaboration includes idea development, feedback, and iterative revision rather than only post-hoc correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial roles in scholarly publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors of scholarly books are of three main types: acquisitions (commissioning) editors, project (production) editors, and copy (manuscript) editors, each with particular responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acquisitions/commissioning editors contract authors; project/production editors manage stages, budgets, and schedules; copy editors prepare copy for printed form. In journals, an editor-in-chief replaces the acquisitions role while production and copy editors remain; 'authors' editor' helps authors prepare manuscripts for submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply publisher style and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary difference between copy editing scholarly books and journals and other sorts of copy editing lies in applying the standards of the publisher to the copy. Most scholarly publishers have a preferred style that usually specifies a particular dictionary and style manual—for example, The Chicago Manual of Style, the MLA Style Manual or the APA Publication Manual in the U.S., or the New Hart's Rules in the U.K.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors must be familiar with and apply the publisher's preferred manuals and house style consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt to multimodality and evolving media
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing has evolved with new forms of media and language that have led to a move towards multimodality; hardcopies and print are no longer the main focus as film and audio require different kinds of edits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should update methods and tools to suit non-print media (audio, video, interactive), recognizing different norms and technical workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity with editing tools and platforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical editing is now more commonly done using applications and websites on devices, which requires editors to be familiar with online platforms like Adobe Acrobat, Microsoft Office, and Google Docs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical competence with common editing software and collaborative platforms is an expectation for modern editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift from surface correction to meaning-based editing
rubrics_metrics.description: While surface-level errors (grammar, spelling) should still be corrected, the focus is shifting towards understanding the meaning of these errors to use the best method to correct them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and teachers should emphasize diagnosing why an error occurred (e.g., word choice vs. ignorance of rules) and choose corrections that preserve meaning and support learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-editing as revision practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-editing is the process of evaluating one's own writing and fixing errors; it is part of the revision process and includes drafting, feedback, and rewriting, important for developing autonomy in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-editing benefits both language learners and native writers; methods include worksheets, apps, and iterative review; it can be effective short-term and complements peer/teacher feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative effectiveness of feedback modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Research shows mixed results: some studies find self-editing more effective short-term than peer-editing; others find peer-dialogue better; automated revising tools paired with peer review lead to greater improvement than automated tools alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use combinations of feedback (peer + automated + teacher) tailored to writer proficiency; be aware that different types of errors respond differently to each feedback mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical editing purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical editing involves reviewing text written on a technical topic, identifying usage errors and ensuring adherence to a style guide. It aims to improve the clarity of the text or message from the author to the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical editing is an umbrella term including policy, integrity, screening, clarification, format, mechanical style, and language edits; editors often need subject familiarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical editing scope (detailed tasks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical editing may include the correction of grammatical mistakes, misspellings, mistyping, incorrect punctuation, inconsistencies in usage, poorly structured sentences, wrong scientific terms, wrong units and dimensions, inconsistency in significant figures, technical ambivalence, technical disambiguation, statements conflicting with general scientific knowledge, correction of synopsis, content, index, headings and subheadings, correcting data and chart presentation in a research paper or report, and correcting errors in citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This detailed checklist shows the broad and specific errors a technical editor should detect and correct; it spans language, structure, data presentation, units, and domain-specific accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Levels/types of edits
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjustments to text can be categorized by different terms within technical editing: policy edits, integrity edits, screening edits, copy clarification edits, format edits and mechanical style edits, language edits, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand and apply appropriate level(s) of edit for the stage of a manuscript—developmental/substantive early, copy/mechanical later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive (developmental) vs copy editing
rubrics_metrics.description: The two most common and broad are substantive editing and copy editing. Substantive editing is developmental because it guides the drafting process by providing essential building blocks to work off of. Copy editing happens later in the drafting process and focuses on changing the text so that it's consistent throughout in terms of accuracy, style, flow, and so on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use substantive editing to shape structure, argument, and content; use copy editing for consistency, grammar, style, and surface polish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential skills for technical editors
rubrics_metrics.description: General essential skills include attention to detail, patience, persistence, the ability to sustain focus while working through lengthy pieces of text on complex topics, tact in dealing with writers, and excellent communication skills. Additionally, language aptitude helps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These interpersonal and cognitive skills are prerequisites for handling complex editorial tasks and for collaborating with authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roles and responsibilities across publishing and newsrooms
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial roles include acquisitions editor, project/production editor, copy editor, journal editor/editor-in-chief, managing editor, and newsroom-specific functions (press/copy editors who ensure accuracy, fairness, and taste, design pages, select stories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different positions have distinct responsibilities (e.g., commissioning, budget/schedule management, shaping content, headline writing); understanding roles helps assign editorial tasks appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paid editing services and specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing services may be provided by firms or freelance editors and can include proofreading, copy editing, online editing, developmental editing, editing for search engine optimization, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and clients should choose services matching project needs; smaller organizations may outsource copy editing to freelancers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual editing categories and techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing visuals can involve photographic and cinematic forms. Modern photo editing techniques include linearization, white balance, noise reduction, tone reproduction and compression. Cinematic editing uses non-linear editing, virtual timelines, and software like DaVinci Resolve or Adobe Premiere Pro.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select techniques and tools appropriate to visual medium; historical context (linear vs non-linear) informs workflow and capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject familiarity for technical editors
rubrics_metrics.description: It helps if the technical editor is familiar with the subject being edited; the 'technical' knowledge that an editor gains over time gives an edge over a newcomer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign editors with domain knowledge for technical documents to better detect substantive errors and ambiguous statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing as a developing profession with limited formal training
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing is a growing field of work in the service industry. There is little career training offered for editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical experience, mentorship, and continuing learning are important; organizations may rely on experienced writers or peer-editing to fulfill editorial needs.
